name: Hinman Glacier / Standard
approach: Park at the Necklace Valley Trailhead (~1,650 ft) at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are deceptively easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail follows the East Fork Foss River through regenerated second-growth forest (logged in the 1930s), entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles. Around the 5-mile mark the trail fords the East Fork Foss River (no bridge — can run high and cold in early-season snowmelt, so plan the crossing for morning low flow) and then turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 2,400 ft over the next 3 miles on steep, root-laced switchbacks into Necklace Valley proper. This section is the approach's real crux for tired legs and pack weight. The trail eases again as it reaches Jade Lake (~4,600 ft, ~8-9 miles), then Emerald Lake a quarter mile beyond, then Opal Lake, threading through the swampy, lake-studded Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water throughout, but buggy in early/mid-summer. From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends; continue cross-country (an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus) up and east roughly 1-1.5 miles and ~1,000+ ft to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes, the standard high camp for the peak (total approach to La Bohn Gap is about 10-11 miles one-way with ~5,000+ ft of cumulative gain). From La Bohn Gap the route continues north-northeast into what remains of the Hinman/Foss Glacier basin — now much diminished and largely bare rock/permanent snowfield rather than a true crevassed glacier in most recent seasons, but still worth crampons/axe and glacier-travel judgment in early season or after a big snow year — then east/east-northeast via easy class 2 ridge/scree scrambling to the summit ridge and along it about half a mile to the true summit (7,492 ft). Loose rock on the final scramble and potential crevasse/bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant (mostly early-season) are the main approach-specific risks beyond the ford and the steep valley headwall.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Necklace Valley trailhead at about 1,650 ft at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first five miles are deceptively flat, gaining only about 600 ft along the East Fork Foss River, entering the wilderness at about 1.5 miles.

Around mile 5 the trail fords the East Fork Foss River — there is no bridge and it runs high and cold in early-season melt, so cross in the morning at low flow. Then it turns uphill in earnest, roughly 2,400 ft over three miles of steep, root-laced switchbacks. This is the real crux of the approach for tired legs.

The grade eases at Jade Lake at about 4,600 ft and eight to nine miles, then Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water, buggy in early summer.

From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends. Continue cross-country on an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus, up and east roughly a mile to a mile and a half and over 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes. That is the standard high camp: about 10 to 11 miles one way with over 5,000 ft of cumulative gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Most parties make it a two or three day trip
hazards: An unbridged ford of the East Fork Foss River around mile 5, high and cold in early-season melt
2,400 ft of steep root-laced switchbacks with a multi-day pack
Crevasse and bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant, mostly early season
Loose rock on the final class 2 scramble
Mosquitoes in the lake basins in early and mid summer
A long walk out from a remote camp if anything goes wrong
approach_variants.baseFinding:
La Bohn Gap and its lakes are the arrival, and the honest finding is that there is no longer much of a glacier to find. Measured in August 2022, the Hinman Glacier had largely disappeared, leaving stranded patches of snow and ice. So do not stand at the gap looking for a glacier front to identify. What you are looking for is the basin above the gap: mostly bare rock and permanent snowfield in most recent seasons, with crevasse and bergschrund hazard only in early season or after a big snow year.

How you know you are at La Bohn Gap: it is where the cairned climbers' path out of the head of Necklace Basin tops out at over 5,500 ft, with the La Bohn Lakes in it. If you are still in swampy lake-studded basin on maintained tread, you have not left Necklace Valley.

Which way from the gap: the summit lies east-northeast of La Bohn Gap, and this route's own recorded positions make that unambiguous — the eastward travel is roughly three times the northward. The first move out of the gap is north-northeast into the basin; after that the line swings east-northeast. A party still heading due north well above the gap is drifting off the route. The objective is the snowfield basin immediately above the lakes, which is unmistakable once you are at the gap, and easy class 2 ridge and scree ground leads from it to the summit ridge.

The final test is a distance along a ridge: from where you gain the summit ridge, the true summit at 7,492 ft is about half a mile along it. A party that tops out on the ridge and stops is half a mile short.

waypoints.name: Necklace Valley Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 68, 4.1 mi from US Hwy 2 at Skykomish; self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 68, about 4.1 miles from US Highway 2 at Skykomish, at roughly 1,650 feet. A self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and a Northwest Forest Pass are required at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River crossing
waypoints.note: Log or ford crossing of the East Fork Foss near an established camp; the first 5 miles gain only ~600 ft but this crossing can be tricky during high runoff.
waypoints.directions: From the trailhead follow Necklace Valley Trail #1062 up the East Fork Foss River. The first 5 miles are nearly flat, gaining only about 600 ft and entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles, to the crossing of the East Fork Foss near an established camp. There is no bridge: cross on logs or ford, ideally in the morning when early-season runoff is lowest.

waypoints.name: Jade Lake
waypoints.note: First of the Necklace Valley lakes and the common base camp for Hinman climbs; trail steepens sharply above the river crossing, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in about 3 miles to reach it.
waypoints.directions: Across the river the trail turns steeply uphill, climbing roughly 2,400 ft in about 3 miles on rooty switchbacks into Necklace Valley. The grade eases at Jade Lake, the first of the valley's lakes.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Gap
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path through boulder fields and heather gains this notch on the ridge crest above La Bohn Lakes; avoid the waterfall drainage to the left, routefinding is poor in fog.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the trail past Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin to its head, where the maintained trail ends. From there a cairned climbers' path climbs through meadow, heather and boulder talus, roughly 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap on the ridge crest above the La Bohn Lakes. Stay out of the waterfall drainage to the left; routefinding is poor in fog.

waypoints.name: Hinman/Foss Glacier remnant snowfield
waypoints.note: Traverse of the shrinking glacier remnant below the west ridge; carry ice axe and crampons/microspikes for firm morning snow, and watch for isolated moats or crevasses late season.
waypoints.directions: From La Bohn Gap head north-northeast into the basin above the gap, then swing east-northeast up the snowfield and glacier remnant below the summit ridge. Carry ice axe and crampons for firm morning snow, and watch for moats or crevasses early in the season.

waypoints.name: Mount Hinman summit
waypoints.note: Broad, multi-humped summit ridge where the true high point is ambiguous; final approach involves a short loose 4th-class scramble near the east end.
waypoints.directions: From the top of the snowfield scramble east up loose scree and broken ridge ground to the broad, multi-humped summit ridge, then follow the crest east to the true high point near its east end.

pitch_detail.notes: 4-5 hours, 2,700 ft gain on maintained trail through dense forest, then off-trail through Emerald Lake valley for final mile
pitch_detail.pitch: Approach (Necklace Valley trailhead to Emerald Lake)

pitch_detail.notes: 1-2 hours, steep waterfall bypass slope is Class 3; loose, broken rock and minimal switchbacks; steep and rooty
pitch_detail.pitch: Off-trail scramble (Emerald Lake to La Bohn Lakes)

pitch_detail.notes: 3-4 hours, 1,500 ft gain through talus, mixed Class 2-3 terrain, heavily fractured summit ridge with questionable footing and 100-500 ft exposure; loose rock throughout
pitch_detail.pitch: Ridge traverse (La Bohn Lakes to summit)
